arXiv:2504.19336v1 [math.NT] 27 Apr 2025

The sequence of partial sums of a unimodular power series is not ultraflat Thanks: 2020 Mathematics Subject Classifications. 11C08, 41A17

Tamás Erdélyi Address: Department of Mathematics, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas 77843, College Station, Texas 77843 Email: terdelyi@tamu.edu
April 23, 2025
Abstract

We show that if (aj)j=0∞(a_{j})_{j=0}^{\infty} is a sequence of numbers aj∈ℂa_{j}\in{\mathbb{C}} with |aj|=1|a_{j}|=1, and

Pn(z)=∑j=0najzj,n=0,1,2,…,P_{n}(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}{a_{j}z^{j}}\,,\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots\,,

then (Pn)(P_{n}) is NOT an ultraflat sequence of unimodular polynomials. This answers a question raised by Zachary Chase.

Keywords: 
polynomials, restricted coefficients, ultraflat sequences of unimodular polynomials, Bernstein factor
††righthead: ultraflat unimodular polynomials

1. Introduction

Let

Kn:={Qn:Qn(z)=∑k=0nakzk,ak∈ℂ,|ak|=1}.{K}_{n}:=\bigg\{Q_{n}:Q_{n}(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{a_{k}z^{k}},\enskip a_{k}\in{\mathbb{C}}\,,\enskip|a_{k}|=1\bigg\}\,.

The class Kn{K}_{n} is called the collection of all complex unimodular polynomials of degree nn. Elements of Kn{K}_{n} may be called Kahane polynomials of degree nn. Let

Ln:={Qn:Qn(z)=∑k=0nakzk,ak∈{−1,1}}.{L}_{n}:=\bigg\{Q_{n}:Q_{n}(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{a_{k}z^{k}},\enskip a_{k}\in\{-1,1\}\bigg\}\,.

The class Ln{L}_{n} is called the collection of all real unimodular polynomials of degree nn. Elements of Ln{L}_{n} are called Littlewood polynomials of degree nn. By Parseval’s formula,

∫02​π|Pn​(ei​t)|2​𝑑t=2​π​(n+1)\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left|P_{n}(e^{it})\right|^{2}\,dt}=2\pi(n+1)

for all Pn∈KnP_{n}\in{K}_{n}. Therefore

mint∈[0,2​π]⁡|Pn​(ei​t)|≤n+1≤maxt∈[0,2​π]⁡|Pn​(ei​t)|.\min_{t\in[0,2\pi]}{\left|P_{n}(e^{it})\right|}\leq\sqrt{n+1}\leq\max_{t\in[0,2\pi]}{\left|P_{n}(e^{it})\right|}\,.

An old problem (or rather an old theme) is the following.

Problem 1.1 (Littlewood's Flatness Problem)

How close can a polynomial Pn∈KnP_{n}\in{K}_{n} or Pn∈LnP_{n}\in{L}_{n} come to satisfying

|Pn​(ei​t)|=n+1,t∈ℝ​?\left|P_{n}(e^{it})\right|=\sqrt{n+1}\,,\qquad t\in{\mathbb{R}}? 1.1

Obviously (1.1) is impossible if n≥1n\geq 1. So one must look for less than (1.1), but then there are various ways of seeking such an “approximate situation”. One way is the following. In his paper [Li1] Littlewood had suggested that, conceivably, there might exist a sequence (Pn)(P_{n}) of polynomials Pn∈KnP_{n}\in{K}_{n} (possibly even Pn∈LnP_{n}\in{L}_{n}) such that (n+1)−1/2|Pn(ei​t)|(n+1)^{-1/2}|P_{n}(e^{it})| converge to 11 uniformly in t∈ℝt\in{\mathbb{R}}. We shall call such sequences of unimodular polynomials “ultraflat”. More precisely, we give the following definition.

Definition 1.2

Given a positive number ε\varepsilon, we say that a polynomial Pn∈KnP_{n}\in{K}_{n} is ε\varepsilon-flat if

(1−ε)​n+1≤|Pn​(ei​t)|≤(1+ε)​n+1,t∈ℝ.(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt{n+1}\leq\left|P_{n}(e^{it})\right|\leq(1+\varepsilon)\sqrt{n+1}\,,\qquad t\in{\mathbb{R}}\,.
Definition 1.3

Given a sequence (εn)(\varepsilon_{n}) of positive numbers tending to 00, we say that a sequence (Pn)(P_{n}) of polynomials Pn∈KnP_{n}\in{K}_{n} is (εn)(\varepsilon_{n})-ultraflat if each PnP_{n} is (εn)(\varepsilon_{n})-flat. We simply say that a sequence (Pn)(P_{n}) of polynomials Pn∈KnP_{n}\in{K}_{n} is ultraflat if it is (εn)(\varepsilon_{n})-ultraflat with a sequence (εn)(\varepsilon_{n}) of positive numbers converging to 00.

The existence of an ultraflat sequence of unimodular polynomials seemed very unlikely, in view of a 1957 conjecture of P. Erdős (Problem 22 in [Er]) asserting that, for all Pn∈KnP_{n}\in{K}_{n} with n≥1n\geq 1,

maxt∈ℝ⁡|Pn​(ei​t)|≥(1+ε)​n+1,\max_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}{\left|P_{n}(e^{it})\right|}\geq(1+\varepsilon)\sqrt{n+1}\,, 1.2

where ε>0\varepsilon>0 is an absolute constant (independent of nn). Yet, refining a method of Körner [Kö], Kahane [Ka] proved that there exists a sequence (Pn)(P_{n}) with Pn∈KnP_{n}\in{K}_{n} which is (εn)(\varepsilon_{n})-ultraflat, where εn=O(n−1/17log⁡n).\varepsilon_{n}=O\left(n^{-1/17}\sqrt{\log n}\right)\,. (Kahane’s paper contained though a slight error which was corrected in [QS2].) Thus the Erdős conjecture (1.2) was disproved for the classes Kn{K}_{n}. For the more restricted class Ln{L}_{n} the analogous Erdős conjecture is unsettled to this date. It is a common belief that the analogous Erdős conjecture for Ln{L}_{n} is true, and consequently there is no ultraflat sequence of polynomials Pn∈LnP_{n}\in{L}_{n}. For an account of some of the work done till the mid 1960’s, see Littlewood’s book [Li2] and [QS2]. Properties of the Rudin-Shapiro polynomials have played a central role in [BBM] as well as in [Er8] to prove a longstanding conjecture of Littlewood on the existence of flat Littlewood polynomials Sn∈LnS_{n}\in{L}_{n} satisfying the inequalities

c1n+1≤|Sn(ei​t)|≤c2n+1,t∈ℝ,n=0,1,2,…,c_{1}\sqrt{n+1}\leq\left|S_{n}(e^{it})\right|\leq c_{2}\sqrt{n+1}\,,\qquad t\in{\mathbb{R}}\,,\quad n=0,1,2,\ldots\,,

with absolute constants c1>0c_{1}>0 and c2>0c_{2}>0. The papers [BB], [Er1]–[Er8], [EN], [Ka], [Od], [QS1], [QS2], and [Sa] deal with topics closely related to ultraflat sequences of unimodular polynomials.

2. New Result

Theorem 2.1

If (aj)j=0∞(a_{j})_{j=0}^{\infty} is a sequence of numbers aj∈ℂa_{j}\in{\mathbb{C}} with |aj|=1|a_{j}|=1, and

Pn(z)=∑j=0najzj,n=0,1,2,…,P_{n}(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}{a_{j}z^{j}}\,,\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots\,,

then (Pn)(P_{n}) is NOT an ultraflat sequence of unimodular polynomials.

In other words, the coefficients of ultraflat unimodular polynomials must vary with the degree. This answers a question raised by Zachary Chase.

Proof of Theorem 2.1

To prove Theorem 2.1 we need the second equality of the following lemma proved in [Er1].

Lemma 2.2 (The Bernstein Factors)

Let qq be an arbitrary positive real number. Let (Pn)(P_{n}) be a fixed ultraflat sequence of polynomials Pn∈KnP_{n}\in{K}_{n}. We have

∫02​π|Pn′​(ei​t)|q​𝑑t∫02​π|Pn​(ei​t)|q​𝑑t=nqq+1+on,q​nq,\frac{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left|P_{n}^{\prime}(e^{it})\right|^{q}\,dt}}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left|P_{n}(e^{it})\right|^{q}\,dt}}=\frac{n^{q}}{q+1}+o_{n,q}n^{q}\,,

with suitable constants on,qo_{n,q} converging to 00 as nn tends to ∞\infty for every fixed q>0q>0, and

max0≤t≤2​π⁡|Pn′​(ei​t)|max0≤t≤2​π⁡|Pn​(ei​t)|=n+on​n\frac{\max_{0\leq t\leq 2\pi}{\left|P_{n}^{\prime}(e^{it})\right|}}{\max_{0\leq t\leq 2\pi}{\left|P_{n}(e^{it})\right|}}=n+o_{n}n

with suitable constants ono_{n} converging to 00 as nn tends to ∞\infty.

Proof of Theorem 2.1

Suppose to the contrary that (aj)j=0∞(a_{j})_{j=0}^{\infty} is a sequence of numbers aj∈ℂa_{j}\in{\mathbb{C}} with |aj|=1|a_{j}|=1,

Pn(z)=∑j=0najzj,n=0,1,2,…,P_{n}(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}{a_{j}z^{j}}\,,\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots\,,

and (Pn)(P_{n}) is an (εn)(\varepsilon_{n})-ultraflat sequence of unimodular polynomials Pn∈KnP_{n}\in{K}_{n}. Associated with Pn∈KnP_{n}\in{K}_{n} we define Q0​(z)≡1Q_{0}(z)\equiv 1 and

Qn+1(z):=1+zn+1Pn(1/z)=1+∑j=1n+1an+1−jzj,n=0,1,2,….Q_{n+1}(z):=1+z^{n+1}P_{n}(1/z)=1+\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}{a_{n+1-j}z^{j}}\,,\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots\,.

Observe that (Qn)(Q_{n}) is an (εn∗)(\varepsilon_{n}^{*})-ultraflat sequence of unimodular polynomials Qn∈KnQ_{n}\in{K}_{n} with positive real numbers εn∗\varepsilon_{n}^{*} converging to 00 and

zn​Qn+1′​(1/z)=zn​∑j=1n+1an+1−j​j​(1/z)j−1=∑j=1n+1an+1−j​j​zn+1−j=∑k=0nak​(n+1−k)​zk,z^{n}Q_{n+1}^{\prime}(1/z)=z^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}{a_{n+1-j}j(1/z)^{j-1}}=\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}{a_{n+1-j}jz^{n+1-j}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{a_{k}(n+1-k)z^{k}}\,,

hence

∑k=0nPk​(z)=∑k=0n(n+1−k)​ak​zk=zn​Qn+1′​(1/z),0≠z∈ℂ.\sum_{k=0}^{n}{P_{k}(z)}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{(n+1-k)a_{k}z^{k}}=z^{n}Q_{n+1}^{\prime}(1/z)\,,\qquad 0\neq z\in{\mathbb{C}}\,. 2.1

Using Definition 1.3 we have

|∑k=0nPk​(ei​t)|≤∑k=0n|Pk​(ei​t)|≤∑k=0n(1+εk)​k+1≤∫1n+2x1/2​𝑑x+∑k=0nεk​(n+1)1/2≤23(1+εn∗⁣∗)(n+2)3/2,t∈ℝ,n=0,1,2,…,\begin{split}\bigg|\sum_{k=0}^{n}{P_{k}(e^{it})}\bigg|&\leq\sum_{k=0}^{n}{\left|P_{k}(e^{it})\right|}\leq\,\sum_{k=0}^{n}{(1+\varepsilon_{k})\sqrt{k+1}}\cr&\leq\int_{1}^{n+2}{x^{1/2}\,dx}+\sum_{k=0}^{n}{\varepsilon_{k}}(n+1)^{1/2}\cr&\leq\frac{2}{3}\,(1+\varepsilon_{n}^{**})(n+2)^{3/2}\,,\qquad t\in{\mathbb{R}}\,,\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots\,,\cr\end{split} 2.2

where

εn∗⁣∗:=32​(n+2)∑k=0nεk,n=0,1,2,…,\varepsilon_{n}^{**}:=\frac{3}{2(n+2)}\sum_{k=0}^{n}{\varepsilon_{k}}\,,\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots\,,

and hence the sequence (εn∗⁣∗)(\varepsilon_{n}^{**}) of positive real numbers converges to 00. On the other hand, combining (2.1) and the second equality of Lemma 2.2 applied to the ultraflat sequence (Qn)(Q_{n}) of unimodular polynomials Qn∈KnQ_{n}\in{K}_{n}, we obtain that there are tn∈[0,2​π)t_{n}\in[0,2\pi) such that

|∑k=0nPk​(ei​tn)|=|Qn+1′​(e−i​tn)|≥34​(n+2)3/2\bigg|\sum_{k=0}^{n}{P_{k}(e^{it_{n}})}\bigg|=\left|Q_{n+1}^{\prime}(e^{-it_{n}})\right|\geq\frac{3}{4}\,(n+2)^{3/2} 2.3

for every sufficiently large nn. Observe that (2.3) contradicts (2.2). ∎
